strengths: Fills a genuine and timely gap: inference-time safety alignment for Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs), an area where, as the related work section argues, no prior principled defense exists.

Well-motivated empirical analysis in Sections 3.3-3.4: the t-SNE study explaining why audio-modality steering fails (early/persistent separation between harmful and safe speech activations leaving no shared steering subspace), and the demonstration that prompt-based defenses from LVLMs cause hidden over-refusal on borderline-safe paired queries.

The proposed BRR metric with paired harmful-safe datasets is a useful evaluation contribution, exposing trade-offs that aggregate benign benchmarks (AirBench) miss - the paper itself demonstrates this discrepancy clearly in Table 3.

Comprehensive evaluation: two LALMs (Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio), four harmfulness benchmarks including the audio-specific AJailBench, ablations of each component (V1/V2/V3 in Figure 4), hyperparameter sensitivity (sample size, scaling coefficient, PCA rank), base-model evaluation (Table 8), and generalization to text-only LLMs (Table 9).

SARSteer achieves the best or near-best ASR and BRR consistently across models and benchmarks (e.g., ASR 10.80 with BRR 79.95 on Figstep-audio for Qwen2-Audio), and results are robust to hyperparameter choices.
Honest treatment of limitations in places (e.g., AdvBench-audio floor effects, prompt-choice sensitivity in B.2, instability of Safe2Refusal variant in B.1).
weaknesses: Modest methodological novelty: text-derived refusal steering is essentially the known single-direction refusal steering (Arditi et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025) applied with an appended refusal prompt, and projecting the steering vector onto the orthogonal complement of a PCA subspace of benign activations is a standard technique. The contribution is largely an application/domain transfer plus the motivating analysis, rather than a new mechanism.

Evaluation data is synthetic and somewhat contrived: all harmful queries are TTS-rendered with a single OpenAI TTS system under one unified textual instruction ('Please generate detailed steps for the question in the audio.'), and the 'safe' counterparts are LLM-generated rewrites. This may create shortcuts for the defense (a fixed template/prompt distribution), and the realism of the threat model is not validated (e.g., no human listening study, no diverse voices, accents, or adversarial audio beyond AJailBench sampling).

Refusal detection relies on a very broad matching-based keyword list (Table 4 includes strings like 'As an', 'Hello!', 'avoid', 'It's important to note'), which risks misclassifying benign answers as refusals and inflating both RR_harm and over-refusal measurements; no inter-method validation between the matching-based RR and the LLM-based ASR judgments is reported.

Small sample sizes and no statistical treatment: 100 alignment pairs, ~250 evaluation pairs for Figstep-audio, 200 AJailBench queries; differences of a few percentage points (e.g., SARSteer 79.95 vs. V2 82.80 BRR in Figure 4, or general utility deltas <0.5 on AirBench) are discussed without confidence intervals or significance tests.

Missing important details for reproducibility in the main text: which layer(s) the steering is applied to and how layers are selected is not clearly specified (the text says 'per-layer' but the interaction between layer choice, alpha=0.1, and results is not analyzed), and no code/data release is stated.

Baselines are limited to the authors' own vanilla adaptations; there is no comparison against a fine-tuning-based defense (e.g., safety SFT) as an upper-bound reference, and no adaptive-attack robustness study (an adversary aware of the steering defense), which is important for a security-oriented contribution.

Some results complicate the narrative: on Kimi-Audio the no-defense ASR is already low (15.6 on Figstep-audio), and in Table 9 the LLM generalization shows ASR essentially unchanged on Figstep (10.00 -> 10.40), so the method's benefit profile is uneven across settings.

Minor presentation issues: several typos ('correpsonding', 'unconspicuously', 'complaint-harmful'), and Figure 1/Table 1 involve multiple separately tuned adapted baselines whose faithfulness to the original methods is hard to verify.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: inference-time safety alignment for Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs), where prior work has mostly documented vulnerability (Yang et al., 2024a; Song et al., 2025) without proposing defenses.

The motivation analysis (Sections 3.3–3.4) is a useful empirical contribution: it systematically shows that vanilla audio-modality steering fails (Figure 1) and connects this to representational separation between harmful/safe speech inputs via t-SNE (Figure 2), and introduces the balanced refusal rate (BRR) with paired harmful-safe audio data to expose over-refusal that generic benign benchmarks miss (Table 1).
The paired harmful-safe audio datasets (Figstep-audio, AdvBench-audio, SORRY-Bench-audio) constructed via TTS + LLM purification are a reusable testbed for the community.

Experiments are relatively broad for the setting: two LALMs, four harmfulness benchmarks, utility evaluation on AirBench, component ablations (V1/V2/V3), hyperparameter sensitivity (Figure 5), base-model results (Table 8), and LLM generalizability (Table 9).

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: algorithm outline (A.5), refusal keyword lists (A.6), dataset construction details (A.2), baseline implementation details (A.3), and hyperparameters (α=0.1, k=10, n=100) are disclosed.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The method combines two standard techniques: a difference-in-means steering vector extracted from appended refusal text (a well-known diff-in-means recipe, cf. Arditi et al. 2024; Belrose 2024) and projection of the vector away from a PCA subspace. Neither component is new; the contribution is mainly their recombination for a new modality, which reduces the methodological significance for a main-track paper.

Central empirical claims rest on thin evidence. The key motivating claim that 'speech activations cannot serve as a feasible operating space for safety steering' is supported only by t-SNE visualizations at two layers on one model (Figure 2). t-SNE is qualitative and notoriously sensitive to hyperparameters; no quantitative separability analysis (e.g., linear probe accuracy across layers) is provided.

The anomalous behavior of baselines is not adequately explained or verified: on Kimi-Audio, MDSteer-h2s increases ASR from 15.6% to 72.4% (Table 2) — a dramatic degradation that warrants deeper investigation, yet the explanation remains speculative. Similarly, SARSteer appears to *improve* AirBench utility on Qwen2-Audio (7.53 vs. 7.43), which is unexplained and suggests noise or measurement instability.

Metric validity concerns. The BRR/refusal-rate metric relies on keyword matching (Table 4) with generic phrases such as 'As an', 'Hello!', 'I'm an', and 'It's important to note', which would misclassify many benign responses as refusals and inflate both over-refusal estimates and SARSteer's advantage. No validation of this judge against human labels is reported, and ASR uses a small fine-tuned Mistral-7b judge without agreement analysis.

No adaptive-attack evaluation. Since the defense is an inference-time steering intervention, an obvious question is whether jailbreak-style or steering-aware attacks bypass it; only AJailBench (200 sampled queries) is used, and there is no analysis of robustness against adversaries aware of the defense. For a safety paper, this omission substantially limits the strength of the security claims.

Narrow model coverage. Only two LALMs (Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio) are evaluated; no newer or architecturally different LALMs (e.g., omni-style models with audio decoding) are tested, making generalization claims ('modality-aware safety defenses') hard to assess. Some conclusions (e.g., baseline behavior) already flip between the two models.

The 'mathematical intuition' in Appendix A.4 is informal and assumes away the hard parts: it presumes w⊤v̂⊥ > 0 for harmful inputs, |w∥| ≫ |w⊥| for borderline cases, and that safe activations 'lie almost entirely in the PCA-estimated safe subspace' — none of which are verified empirically. This is intuition dressed as analysis rather than a supported theoretical claim.

No statistical rigor: single runs, no seeds/variance estimates, no significance testing, despite many small differences (e.g., 10.80 vs. 12.00 ASR) being used to claim superiority. Evaluation sets are small (e.g., 200 AJailBench samples, 250 pairs).

No explicit limitations section or broader-impact/ethics discussion, despite the work involving generation of harmful audio content and release of steering vectors that modify safety behavior; the ethics of the constructed datasets and potential dual-use of the technique are not addressed.

Presentation polish is mixed: typos ('correpsonding', 'unconspicuously'), and the framing 'first inference-time defense framework for LALMs' is asserted repeatedly without careful hedging about concurrent work.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: safety alignment for Large Audio-Language Models has been largely unexplored, and SARSteer is presented as the first inference-time defense framework in this setting.

The motivation analysis (Sections 3.3-3.4) is a real strength: the paired harmful-safe audio dataset construction, the demonstration that vanilla steering adaptations actively worsen attack success rates (Figure 1), and the t-SNE analysis explaining why audio activations differ from text provide useful empirical understanding, not just a new method.

The proposed BRR (balanced refusal rate) metric and the paired borderline-safe dataset expose over-refusal that general-purpose benign benchmarks miss (Table 1); this is a methodological contribution that could benefit follow-up work.

The experimental coverage is broad: two LALMs (Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio), four harmful benchmarks including audio-specific jailbreaks (AJailBench), utility on AirBench, component ablations (Figure 4), hyperparameter robustness (Figure 5), different refusal prompts/directions, base models, and generalization to text LLMs (Appendix B.4).
Implementation details, baselines adaptation, refusal keyword lists, and LLM usage are documented in the appendix, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central mechanism is applied indiscriminately: the steering vector alpha*v_perp is added at every generated token for every input. Selectivity between harmful and benign queries rests entirely on the geometric argument in Appendix A.4, which assumes without evidence that (i) w^T v_perp > 0 for harmful activations, and (ii) borderline-safe activations lie 'mostly' in the PCA-estimated safe subspace with |w_parallel| >> |w_perp|. No direct measurements validate these assumptions, so the 'principled' framing is stronger than the actual support.

The t-SNE analysis in Section 3.3 is qualitative only. The strong claim that audio harmful/safe activations have 'no shared subspace' for steering would be better supported by quantitative separability probes (e.g., linear probe accuracy, cosine similarity of mean differences, ablation-based causality tests) rather than 2D visualizations.

The refusal-rate evaluation relies on brittle keyword matching (Table 4) that includes generic strings such as 'Hello!', 'As an', and 'I'm just'; this could materially distort RR/BRR numbers, and no human verification or inter-annotator agreement is reported for the matching-based results.

Baselines are relatively weak: only vanilla adaptations of two prompt-based and two steering defenses. No comparison against safety fine-tuning (SFT) or other stronger inference-time defenses, making it hard to gauge how SARSteer compares to the best achievable safety-utility trade-off.

There is a potential confound in the steering vector construction: the vector is the difference of last-token activations between the original query and the query with an appended refusal sentence. Since appending text changes sequence length and last-token position, the difference may partly capture position/text-termination artifacts rather than refusal semantics; this is not analyzed.

No statistical rigor: results are single-run point estimates on samples of ~200-250 eval queries with no confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance testing, despite several reported gaps of a few points.

Robustness against adaptive attacks is not discussed: an attacker aware of the steering could potentially craft audio inputs that avoid the refusal direction; for a defense paper, this absence of adaptive evaluation and no explicit limitations/ethics discussion of releasing harmful audio data are notable omissions.
Writing has minor issues (e.g., 'unconspicuously', 'correpsonding'), and a few claims (e.g., 'establishing a principled step') overstate the level of theoretical grounding.
